guideTitle: Best Inkjet Printers for Home Use (2026)
metaTitle: Best Inkjet Printers for Home Use in 2026
metaDescription: Six cartridge inkjet printers for home use compared on duplex, feeders, display, photo ability and ink upkeep, with honest picks for families and students.
expertTake: The HP Envy 6155 is the best all-round home inkjet because it adds automatic duplex and a decent tray to a small body. The HP DeskJet 2955 is the value pick for someone who prints a few color pages a month. Anyone who prints daily should skip cartridge inkjets and look at an ink tank or a laser.
introParagraphs: A cartridge inkjet sprays tiny droplets of liquid ink onto the page, which makes it the most flexible home printer: it handles color documents, school projects and photos on a single machine and costs little to buy. That flexibility is why it remains the default family printer.

The catch is running cost. Small cartridges empty quickly, and a printhead that sits idle can dry out. The differences that matter are duplex, whether a feeder is included, how ink is supplied and how well the machine copes with long gaps between jobs.

products.name: HP Envy 6155 Wireless Duplex All-in-One Inkjet
products.description:
HP's Envy 6155 is aimed at households, and its main selling point is automatic two-sided printing in a body that stays small. A 100-sheet input tray is double the paper of the DeskJet class, so a school packet or a hobby project does not stall on a refill.

The tradeoff is ink cost. Like every cartridge inkjet, it uses small cartridges that run out sooner than a tank would, and the Instant Ink trial in the listing is a subscription that bills by page count, so read the terms before enrolling. If you print more than a few dozen pages a month, the Canon MegaTank G3270 will cost far less per page.

Ownership is easier if you keep the head wet. Print a page every week or two, keep the paper dry and run a head cleaning only when lines appear, because each cleaning uses ink. A printer that sees steady light use does well here, and the duplex unit keeps paper costs down for homework printing.
products.bestFor: Families that print schoolwork and want automatic two-sided output.

100-sheet tray doubles the entry class

Print, scan and copy in one machine

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS6520 Wireless Inkjet with OLED Display
products.description:
The TS6520 is Canon's mid-tier home inkjet, with a 1.42 inch OLED display that shows setup and status instead of the blinking lights of the cheapest models. The listing highlights a two-cartridge system, one black and one color, which keeps replacement simple but means a single empty color tower ends a color print.

The catch is that the two-cartridge design is cheap to run only if you print mostly in one color mode. A heavy color user will empty the tri-color cartridge fast, and the Canon PIXMA TS4320 shares the same cartridge approach with fewer features. The display is a real step up from lights, but it is small.

Ownership is simple: swap a cartridge when the display tells you, print a page weekly and keep the cover shut. Canon's app handles wireless setup, and firmware changes can alter how non-original ink is treated, so check before buying third-party cartridges. For a student or a household, this is a calm, no-surprise printer.
products.bestFor: Households that want a clear display and straightforward cartridges.
pros: OLED display replaces blinking status lights
Two-cartridge design is easy to refill

Print, scan and copy included
cons: Single color cartridge ends all color printing when empty
No automatic duplex in the listing
Small display is not a touchscreen

products.name: Canon PIXMA TR4720 4-in-1 Wireless Inkjet with ADF
products.description:
The TR4720 is Canon's home office inkjet, adding an automatic document feeder and fax to the basic print, scan and copy functions. The listing quotes a power draw of 7 watts in use and 0.8 watts in standby, which is useful for a printer that sits powered all day.

The downside is that it is still a cartridge inkjet, so ink cost per page is the same weakness as its siblings, and it lacks the Canon TS6520's display. A feeder helps with multi-page forms, but fax is a feature many homes never use. For a student or a home worker who scans stacks, the feeder is the reason to choose it.

Ownership follows Canon's cartridge routine. Install is designed to be simple, and the weekly test print keeps the head clear. Since the machine does a lot at a low price tier, expect to pay for it in ink over time, so consider how much you print before committing.
products.bestFor: Home workers who scan multi-page forms and want a feeder cheaply.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS4320 Wireless Inkjet All-in-One
products.description:
Canon's TS4320 is the entry all-in-one of the family, offering the same two-cartridge system as the TS6520 without the display. The listing calls it a cost-efficient multifunction for home and hybrid workers, and its easy setup from a phone is the selling point.

The cost against the TS6520 is the interface: with no screen you rely on lights and the phone app. Against the Canon TR4720, you give up the feeder and fax. If your printing is occasional, that is a sensible trade, and the savings go to ink.

Ownership is the same as any entry inkjet: replace cartridges as they empty, print a page weekly, avoid long storage with the heads uncovered and check firmware notes on third-party ink. A simple design means few surprises, and it will serve a household that prints a few pages a week for years.
products.bestFor: Households that print a few pages a week and want a low entry cost.

products.name: HP DeskJet 2955 Wireless All-in-One Inkjet
products.description:
HP aims the DeskJet 2955 at basic needs: to-do lists, letters and financial forms in color, with a 60-sheet input tray and wireless printing from a phone. It sits at the very bottom of the HP price ladder in this lineup, and the engineering is what you would expect: a small head, a light chassis and few extras.

The tradeoff is limits. There is no duplex, a small tray means frequent reloads and the paper path is built for plain paper rather than thick stock. Against the HP Envy 6155, you give up duplex and the larger tray, which is the whole point of the price gap.

Ownership is easy if you print rarely, but the cartridges are small and can run out fast. Print a page every week or two to keep the head wet, keep a spare set and consider the cost of ink before you buy. For a first printer or a drawer printer, it does the job.
products.bestFor: Light users who want a color printer for the lowest outlay.
pros: Lowest entry cost in this lineup
Light enough to move between rooms

Print, scan and copy in one body

products.name: Brother Work Smart 1360 Wireless Duplex Inkjet
products.description:
Brother's Work Smart 1360 packs automatic duplex and a 20-sheet document feeder into a compact home model, a combination the HP Envy 6155 and Canon TS6520 do not offer. Cloud app connections let you print from and scan to services like Google Drive and Dropbox from the printer itself.

What you give up is the ink system. It is still a cartridge inkjet, so the running cost is above a tank, and the feeder is a 20-sheet unit, good for short documents only. It occupies the upper-middle of the lineup by price tier, so it is not the cheapest route to duplex.

Ownership follows the usual inkjet pattern: print weekly, replace cartridges promptly and keep the lid closed. Brother drivers are straightforward and the feeder is handy for a home worker. A house with a student and a remote worker will get the most from the pairing of duplex and feeder.
products.bestFor: Home workers who want duplex and a feeder in one inkjet.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A cartridge inkjet is cheap to buy and costly to run, because small cartridges yield few pages. Divide the replacement price by its yield before you buy, and notice that the Canon TS4320 and TS6520 use a single tri-color cartridge, so one empty color ends all color printing. For heavy printers a tank is cheaper.

The HP Envy 6155 and Brother Work Smart 1360 have automatic duplex, while the HP DeskJet 2955 does not and holds only 60 sheets. Duplex halves paper for homework, and a 100-sheet tray on the Envy avoids reloads. Match these to your usual job.

A feeder lets you scan or copy stacks without lifting the lid each time. The Canon TR4720 has one and the Brother Work Smart 1360 has a 20-sheet feeder. Fax is rarely needed, so do not pay for it unless a client asks.
Inkjet heads dry if the printer sits unused, and cleaning cycles use ink. Print a page every week or two to keep nozzles wet. If you print only a few times a year, a laser is the better tool.

HP's Instant Ink subscription bills by page count and can lock the printer to the plan, so read the terms. Firmware updates can also change how non-original cartridges are treated. Choose a model whose cartridge policy you can live with.

These printers handle color documents well, but a two-cartridge model blends colors in one tri-color tank, so photos are decent rather than gallery grade. For better photo quality look at a six-ink photo printer.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ink and running cost
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the cartridge design on each model, from the two-cartridge Canon TS6520 to the HP plan terms. Cost per page matters more than the box price. We flagged subscription lock-in as a risk.

howWeEvaluated.title: Paper handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared duplex, tray size and feeder presence, with the HP Envy 6155 offering a 100-sheet tray and the Brother Work Smart 1360 a 20-sheet feeder. Models without duplex lost points. Simple paths scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Interface and setup
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed the OLED display on the Canon TS6520 against the light-only Canon TS4320. App setup and cloud features counted for ease of use. A clear status display reduces support calls.

howWeEvaluated.title: Household fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched machines to use, from the HP DeskJet 2955 for light use to the Canon TR4720 for stack scanning. Body size and noise were considered. Features that sit unused were not rewarded.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership risk
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered idle clogging, firmware policy on third-party ink and warranty. The need for weekly use was noted for every cartridge inkjet. Long-term cost was weighed over three years.

cards.label: Cartridge inkjet
cards.text: A cartridge inkjet like the HP Envy 6155 is cheap to buy and tolerates occasional use. Ink costs more per page and cartridges run out sooner.

cards.label: Ink tank
cards.text: A tank printer costs more upfront but brings the cost per page far lower, as in the Canon MegaTank G3270. It rewards weekly printing and punishes long idle gaps.

howToChoose.note: Pick a cartridge inkjet if you print little; pick a tank if you print weekly.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Homework means long documents, two-sided pages and a tray that does not run dry mid-job. Automatic duplex and a tray of at least 100 sheets matter more than photo quality.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The HP Envy 6155 is the clearest fit, with duplex and a 100-sheet tray. The Brother Work Smart 1360 adds a feeder for copying worksheets.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you print weekly, where duplex on the HP Envy 6155 or Brother Work Smart 1360 saves paper, or if a feeder on the Canon TR4720 saves scanning time.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you print a few pages a month, where the HP DeskJet 2955 or Canon TS4320 gives color and scanning at the lowest tier.

maintenance.why: Keeps all nozzles wet and avoids clogs. A short test page is enough.
Running dry can let air into the head and ruin it. Keep a spare set.
Cleaning uses ink, so do it only when a nozzle check shows gaps.
Damp paper curls and jams in duplex. Store the ream sealed.
Dust creates lines on scans. A dry cloth is enough.

faq.q: Is an inkjet or a laser better for home use?
faq.a: An inkjet handles color and photos and costs little to buy, so it suits a family that prints variety. A laser is better for black text and long idle gaps.

faq.q: Why is inkjet ink so expensive?
faq.a: Small cartridges hold little ink and the printer is priced low, so the maker earns on supplies. Divide the replacement price by its yield to see the real cost per page.

Yes, if they sit for weeks. Ink at the nozzle evaporates and leaves a plug, so streaks and missing colors are the first sign. A weekly test page keeps the head wet, and a head cleaning clears small clogs, though each cleaning spends ink you paid for.

faq.q: Is duplex worth having on a home inkjet?
faq.a: If you print homework or reports, yes, because it halves paper use. For single pages it adds cost you will not use.

faq.q: Should I join a subscription ink plan?
faq.a: Only if your printing is steady and the plan fits your page count. Read the terms, because some plans lock the printer to the subscription, and cancelling can leave the machine refusing ordinary cartridges until the plan state is cleared.

faq.q: Can an inkjet print good photos?
faq.a: A two-cartridge model prints decent snapshots, but a six-ink photo printer or a tank with photo ink does better. Check the model specs before expecting gallery prints.
